title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase (3.97 vs 3.83)
drivers.evidence: Two consecutive weeks at 3.97 saw median sales x0.86 vs baseline; implies 14% demand drop from price hike.

drivers.name: TikTok trend
drivers.evidence: Unproven driver; no past TikTok effect seen. Shrink upward lift toward 1.0 due to low confidence and noise.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.2. No events or promotions are scheduled, but the price is raised 3.7% above regular. Recent weeks show a dip after price increases: x0.86 at 3.97 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05), suggesting a downside effect. The product is trending on TikTok, a novel driver with no past parallel. Past promotions averaged x1.82 (noise-adjusted), but this is not a promotion. The classical model suggests no uplift, but judgment overrides it: the TikTok trend is untested, so shrink the effect. The price increase likely reduces demand. Combine downward price effect with uncertain TikTok lift. Shrink both toward 1.0.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.2 | 5%-95%: 77.5 - 200.3 | 10%-90%: 89.0 - 170.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
